Why it matters: The American icon's latest cause underscores how the politics surrounding AI infrastructure are beginning to resemble the last decade's fights over fossil fuels.

"The last thing we need is a loud, water thieving, light polluting, data center anywhere near our town (or any others for that matter)," Nelson told his more than one million Instagram followers recently.

Flashback: "For 29 years, corporations have continued to take the land away from the small family farmers, and this is what we're here to fight against," Nelson said during a 2014 Nebraska concert held to oppose the Keystone XL pipeline.

"We always listen to our Yoda," joked Nebraskan activist Jane Kleeb, referring to Nelson.

  • A leader of Nebraska's fight against the now-canceled Keystone XL pipeline, today Kleeb is active in the largely decentralized opposition to AI infrastructure.

The big picture: Data centers represent one of the fastest-growing, most bipartisan infrastructure backlashes in years.

  • "We just want to make sure when these massive infrastructure projects are being built, that they're not leaving harms in the communities that will live with them forever," said Kleeb, who is co-founder of the nonprofit Bold Alliance and chair of the Nebraska Democratic Party.

How it works: The parallels between the fossil fuel sector and data centers are striking.

  • Tech companies have been touting how essential data centers are to our lives, which echoes how fossil fuel companies remind us we use oil and natural gas to move around.
  • Kleeb says many developers approach communities with a "tech bro" mentality that leaves residents feeling unheard.

What they're saying: "You don't get your social license to operate by telling everybody how they're going to do better economically," said Kevin Book, managing director at the nonpartisan research firm ClearView Energy Partners, whose clients include institutional investors and corporate leaders.

  • "You get it by listening to their concerns and helping them process emotions."

Between the lines: Both fights are also proxies for larger fears: Data centers are to AI what fossil fuel infrastructure is to climate change.

  • "What's interesting is they are both linked to this other obvious threat to people," said Michael Lazarus, senior scientist emeritus at the climate research group Stockholm Environment Institute. "Both are existential in their own way."

Friction point: Tech companies often say a few unnamed "bad actors" give everyone a bad reputation on data centers.

  • "Pipeline companies used to say this, too," Kleeb said. "If that's true, name them and put out a set of policy suggestions that you believe are the proper guardrails around data centers."

The other side: That might be in the works, according to Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition.

  • "We are in the process of honing in on how to better demonstrate our commitments to these principles for responsible development," Diorio told Axios.
  • Those include open dialogues with communities, paying their fair share of power costs and efficiently using water, he added.
  • "One of the things that is very clear from the industry perspective is that we're catching up," said Diorio, whose group represents roughly 50 companies across the value chain of AI.

Reality check: The comparison between data centers and fossil fuels isn't perfect, of course. For one, this cycle of opposition has developed faster and is more widespread.

  • "It took us years to build our coalitions," Kleeb said of her days fighting the Keystone pipeline.

Stunning stat: In just three months, Texas' Republican Governor Greg Abbott went from welcoming data centers to imposing a pause while new rules are considered.

  • "What happened in Texas and the governor is shocking in how quickly his posture changed," said Timothy Fox, an analyst who works with Book at ClearView Energy Partners.

What we're watching: Data centers are solidified as a top flashpoint in this year's midterm elections. Fox expects them to be "the most pressing energy topic before state legislatures next year."

Zoom in: More state lawmakers are likely to consider imposing rules on power and water, along with repealing tax credits, Fox said.

  • "It would be very difficult for lawmakers to argue that these companies with their significant financial wherewithal require tax exemption while the general public views data centers as the primary culprit for rising power prices," Fox said.

Zoom out: That's what happened with fossil fuels. States responded with stricter fracking regulations and, in some cases, higher taxes rather than shutting the industry down, Book said. Even after Keystone XL was canceled, most fossil fuel development continued.

The bottom line: The fossil fuel industry had years to respond to growing local opposition. The AI industry may have only a matter of months.

item.title: AI scrambles the political map
item.description:
The search for a winning message on AI is pushing candidates and lawmakers into unexpected political territory.

Why it matters: With the midterms approaching, AI is creating alliances across party lines while opening fissures within them.

Here are three ways AI is scrambling the political map.

1. Centrist Democrats versus progressives on data centers

New York made waves as the first state to impose a data center moratorium — a product of Gov. Kathy Hochul joining forces with progressive state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez. But the two policymakers are just getting started on reconciling their differing approaches to AI.

  • Gonzalez previously advocated for a three-year moratorium and is working to extend the one-year pause in Hochul's executive order. She's spearheading a statewide tour to advocate for Hochul to sign her Responsible Data Center Development Act.
  • Gonzalez is going beyond Democratic strongholds, with her tour reaching into red and purple parts of upstate New York and the Hudson Valley.
  • Where Hochul and Gonzalez land is an early test of just how much progressive and centrist Democrats can align on an issue that's mobilizing voters across the political spectrum.

What they're saying: "We need Gov. Hochul to step up and sign the bill and provide full protection to the people of New York," Sustainable Finger Lakes president Gay Nicholson said in a call with reporters ahead of the tour.

  • "Please just don't leave our small rural towns with limited staff and resources at the mercy of an extractive industry that enriches themselves at the expense of upstate New Yorkers," said Nicholson, whose organization is among those advocating for Gonzalez's bill.

Zoom out: For a brief moment, Hochul and President Trump were sounding similar, until Hochul took it a step further with her moratorium executive order.

  • "If Hochul is serious about lowering costs, she should embrace the Trump Administration's energy agenda," a White House official told Axios in a statement following the signing of Hochul's executive order. "Democrats want to stifle innovation and weaken America's competitive edge over China in the AI race."

2. Trump world versus Tea Party advocates on data centers

Activists with ties to the Tea Party movement are protesting data centers, calling on Republicans to "get their heads out of the sand and stop pretending like this is not an issue, because it is an issue," Humans First spokesperson Chris Barron said.

  • Humans First describes itself as a grassroots conservative organization fighting for an "America First AI policy," and its chair, Amy Kremer, is a longtime Tea Party figure.
  • The group, however, is being disavowed by conservative outlets and facing accusations of being an astroturf organization aligned with the left.

The intrigue: Barron, a Trump surrogate in 2016, pushed back against criticism that liberals holding anti-Trump signs showed up at data center protests last month organized by Humans First, noting that "the foundational building blocks" of MAGA included converting people into Republican voters.

  • "We've been loyal supporters of the president from the very beginning," Barron said, adding, "I feel confident that at the end of the day, the president will understand what the base of his party wants."

The other side: While Humans First says it represents the MAGA base and conservatives, sources familiar with the administration say there's no alignment with the organization.

  • "There is no one in this group that has any access, visibility, or influence in the White House at all," one source told Axios, referring to Humans First.

3. Libertarians and progressives on surveillance

Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) has begun strategizing for a Democratic takeover of the House, eyeing common ground with libertarian lawmakers on the right.

  • The two factions have historically aligned on surveillance, but AI is giving the issue a bigger playing field, and congressional leaders like Casar plan to take advantage.
  • Casar is focusing on privacy and closing surveillance law loopholes that allow brokers to collect data from Americans through corporations.
  • In places like Pennsylvania and West Virginia, Republicans are zeroing in on AI-powered surveillance and joining Democrats on legislation to create safeguards against government and industry misuse of personal data.

The bottom line: Don't look for clean Republican-versus-Democratic platforms on AI ahead of the elections.

item.title: GOP finds its next progressive target in Minnesota
item.description:
Republicans have a new name on their growing list of progressive midterm targets: Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, fresh off a landslide Senate primary win.

Why it matters: With President Trump's approval ratings in the 30s, Republicans are trying to turn the midterms from a referendum on him into a choice between the GOP and a Democratic Party they argue has moved sharply to the left.

  • That means portraying some progressive Democrats who've won statewide primaries as national foils. The strategy came into focus last week, after Abdul El-Sayed's victory in Michigan's Senate primary.

Republicans will aim to make El-Sayed and liberal podcaster Hasan Piker into focal points of their upcoming midterm convention in Dallas.

  • GOP operatives have been collecting video of El-Sayed, Piker and other prominent liberals for use in attack reels at the Sept. 9-10 convention.
  • Trump already has attacked El-Sayed over his Muslim faith, accusing Democrats after his win of nominating "jihadists" — which liberals denounced as Islamophobic.

Now, Republicans are zeroing in on Flanagan.

  • After Tuesday's primary, the conservative X account End Wokeness posted a video of Flanagan wearing a hijab, which she had worn during a 2025 visit to a mosque. Pro-Trump activist Jack Posobiec posted a link to a story that included a picture of Flanagan wearing a "protect trans kids" T-shirt.
  • The National Republican Senatorial Committee released a video describing her as an "extremist."

Zoom in: GOP operatives see lines of attack in Flanagan's support for dismantling ICE and support for transgender rights, and her ties to progressive Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders.

  • Republicans also plan to tout the Minnesota fraud scandals that unfolded during Flanagan's tenure as lieutenant governor as evidence of liberal mismanagement.

State of play: Republicans haven't won a statewide race in Minnesota in two decades, and limited spring polling showed Flanagan leading the GOP's Senate nominee, former NFL reporter Michele Tafoya.

  • National GOP strategists are watching the race closely to measure how much to invest in it.

Tafoya has been invited to a donor retreat in California later this month that will be hosted by the pro-GOP Senate Leadership Fund's super PAC.

  • Republicans grew more bullish about Tafoya's chances Tuesday after state House Speaker Lisa Demuth won Minnesota's GOP primary for governor over MyPillow founder Mike Lindell, an election conspiracy theorist whom GOP operatives feared would have alienated independents and dragged down the party's ticket.
  • Even if Republicans can't defeat Flanagan, they hope to force Democrats to spend resources defending the seat being vacated by Amy Klobuchar, who won the Democratic primary for governor.

Yes, but: Republicans face a tough political environment in Minnesota, where Trump has a 37% approval rating.

  • Flanagan showed political strength in the primary, defeating a better-funded and more moderate Democratic opponent by 20 points.
  • Republicans are also grappling with fallout from the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis by federal immigration officers deployed there by Trump's administration.

The other side: Flanagan is tying Tafoya to Trump, including by highlighting Tafoya's comments that Minnesotans should "take one less trip to Starbucks" and accept temporary economic pain during the U.S.-Iran war.

"Republicans can throw around false labels all they want, but it won't distract Minnesotans from the reality that Donald Trump is abusing his authority every single day, while his failed economy makes life harder for working families," a Flanagan spokesperson Lexi Byler told Axios.

  • Tafoya "would be just another loyal vote for Trump," Byler added, "and Minnesotans will reject her just as they have rejected him."
